body: Part of this problem is definitely the drawback we discussed about using depth instead of euclidean distance, but there seems to be something else wrong that is also causing an issue. I have some ideas but it might take some time, as I'm a away for awhile.
Will take a look too. OP seems to say that the problem occurs when the camera is *inside* the occluder. It may be a corner case that we haven't anticipated.

I just spent 30mins playing with the MRP.

I couldn't reproduce any visual glitch when the camera is **outside** the occluder.
👉 This issue should not affect the vast majority of users.

When the camera is **inside** though, it's true that the culling behavior of objects outside is less consistent than before.
But it is the price we decided to pay in #103798 for increased performance and other benefits : see discussions in #97712 and #100907.

Now, the question is what are the use cases that would require visual consistency from inside occluders ?
Usually occluders plays together with geometry and colliders, so you do not render from inside anyway.

@eigenviolet it may help if you can say more on your use case and what's the purpose of rendering from inside.

> I still notice that objects don't get culled from all angles and positions in both 4.4 and 4.5

There is nothing wrong some objects don't get culled under certain circumstances. Lesser is better, but Godot's occlusion culling has tradeoffs and this is one of them. The opposite (visible objects popping out) would be much more concerning.
Yeah, I guess this bug report was kinda stupid, so I might close it

I'm reopening this issue as I think the response might have been made a bit hastily and without proper analysis. 

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/103798 was made to improve precision for distant objects at the cost of performance. When it was merged, nobody actually tested performance and confirmed how much of a difference it made, which was a mistake given the fact that we had originally rejected this approach due to performance concerns (see https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/97712#issuecomment-2420095864).

Now we have a user saying that this approach has caused an extremely visible and obvious regression. We need to add least do some due diligence and measure the performance difference and figure out if the theoretical decrease in cost for depth queries is outweighed by the increase in cost from under-occluding. Hand waving and saying that performance decreases are expected is not sufficient. 

> Now, the question is what are the use cases that would require visual consistency from inside occluders ?
Usually occluders plays together with geometry and colliders, so you do not render from inside anyway.

Typically when you create an occluder for a building you use a single occluder and view it both from inside and outside. The MRP may be extreme since the boxOccluder is not that big, but its not unreasonable for someone to expect that occluders are double sided

Btw, the specific line of the commit that caused this issue seems to be this line where it picks the AABB's closest corner for the min_depth value:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/18eb1c1072eba9032efb35a3b6e1039511700548/servers/rendering/renderer_scene_occlusion_cull.h#L87

 I agree with that comment on https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/97712#issuecomment-2420095864 that the best solution would be if there is some way to get the point where the camera frustum intersects with the AABB and use that when the corner is outside the frustum.

> When it was merged, nobody actually tested performance and confirmed how much of a difference it made

I agree #103798 would have needed some performance benchmark before merged. What's not trivial though is that the amount of under-occlusion would largely depend on the scene. I'm wondering whether Godot's test project `occlusion_culling_mesh_lod` is a good candidate.

> I agree with that comment on #97712 (comment) that the best solution would be if there is some way to get the point where the camera frustum intersects with the AABB and use that when the corner is outside the frustum.

Computing the intersection would likely mean transforming the AABB back and forth to clip space. It's just gut at this stage but if this issue turns out to be a real blocker for some users, then moving the occlusion buffer back to Euclidean distance would be cheaper and provide equivalent (if not superior) results visually than trying to compute the intersection. Of course we would then loose the support of very far objects.

> Will take a look too. OP seems to say that the problem occurs when the camera is _inside_ the occluder. It may be a corner case that we haven't anticipated.

The fallback case for a camera being inside an occlusion volume should always trigger a conservative 'we cant use this occluder' result in my opinion.

I'm not sure what type of visual result is expected from putting a camera inside an occluder either by accident or intentionally.

If the game camera is clipping into walls or objects with occluders placed in them, that's on their camera code to keep it out of this happening, or at a minimum 'turn off an occluder if we are bumping into/clipping thru it'.
This is the safe thing to do regardless of whether its an analytical geometry occlusion method or a conservative rasterization based approach.

There has to be some level of responsibility + usage rules placed on devs using an occlusion system. And on the engine side it needs to have a 'safe mode' thats lenient towards camera intersections.

Officially documenting some more best practices for their usage in common game scenarios where they are useful (city racing games / indoors / fps) is probably a good idea if people are reporting weird visual rendering results because they dont understand this interaction between the camera and occlusion culling.

> The fallback case for a camera being inside an occlusion volume should always trigger a conservative 'we cant use this occluder' result in my opinion.

Why is that? In Godot occluders are double sided geometry. The engine has no concept of being inside an occluder, in either case we are just rasterizing triangles to a depth buffer. 

> I'm not sure what type of visual result is expected from putting a camera inside an occluder either by accident or intentionally.

In the MRP, I think its fair to expect that pretty much all geometry gets culled except for where the camera plane intersects with the occlusion geometry. 

But in any case, I don't think the problem has to do with being _inside_ an occluder at all. The problem is that we are now failing to render occluding triangles when the camera gets close to them. Which means that any game set inside a building is going to fail to occlude a lot of things that should be trivial.

> > The fallback case for a camera being inside an occlusion volume should always trigger a conservative 'we cant use this occluder' result in my opinion.
> 
> Why is that? In Godot occluders are double sided geometry. The engine has no concept of being inside an occluder, in either case we are just rasterizing triangles to a depth buffer.

There is no mention in the documentation about occluders being double-sided.
I'm not familiar with the implementation details in the engine and I only have my experiences of using occlusion culling in other engines and games which treated them as single-sided.
If the godot engine has no concept of being 'in an occluder' because the objects are just handed over to embree and they are considered double sided, then that helps me understand the issues at hand.

@snowflower changing the camera's z-far (view->settings) to something closer (default is 4000) should give something more akin to the gradient mapped depth visualization that you expected.

> I don't think the problem has to do with being inside an occluder at all. The problem is that we are now failing to render occluding triangles when the camera gets close to them.

I managed to narrow the problem further down.
First, occluding geometry is rendered correctly in the buffer. The issue doesn't come from this.

Second, it's indeed not related to being inside the occluder, but rather to the position of the occludees relative to the occluder: the exact same issue can be reproduced with a Quad occluder (with no inside).
Being inside amplifies the issue as the occluder's backfaces are most likely closer to the occludee than its front faces.

Third, it's definitely a consequence of moving occlusion tests from Euclidian distance to Z-depth. The algorithm takes the closest Z amongst the 8 occludee's world space AABB corners, and compares it to a hierarchical Z buffer across the occludee's screen space AABB footprint.
In cases the buffer's Z varies a lot across the occludee's footprint (e.g. when the Quad occluder is significantly off the XY view space plane), it may happen that it exceeds the occludee's closest Z at some point. This is especially likely when the occludee's closest AABB corner is close to the occluder AND the occludee has a wide footprint in screen space.
*Edit : Note that this also happens with Euclidian buffer especially on large occludees. On smaller ones, the occluder plane has to be off-XY by at least 45 degrees given how Euclidian distance works to become subject to significant under-occlusion.*

Next step is putting a MRP together that will allow to precisely trace the issue and see whether there is anything else going on.

The default wireframe representation of the occluder instance is not useful enough when the camera is about to clip thru them,
so I assigned a matching meshInstance3D shape with a semitransparent material to visually assist in looking at the issue.


![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/bb244a82-8197-4e0f-bd2e-9f3b313e8248)

It makes it more visually apparent when there is a situation of the camera near clip slicing into the camera facing occlusion geometry, which means the occlusion rasterization buffer is only drawing the back facing sections of the clipped away front-face area.
At 13 seconds into my video here I intentionally place the camera into the occluder partially, so the occlusion rasterization cant draw the front face completely.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ddf0cb2d-b0b4-423f-a040-e913c19de73a


At this specific frame in the video, the front face of the occluder clips away, and the sphere is visible because the sphere occludee 's conservative bounding volume test fails against the contents of the occlusion buffer that has only the occluder's backface polygon depth for a large part of the buffer.

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e5b41261-e4ce-4ceb-bf7d-6bf7dcd84018)


Again I don't see this creating false occlusion when the camera is outside an occluder.
In the case of the side walls being successfully occluded that you see on the left and right edges of the frustum when you have the entire occluder in your camera view up against the near clip plane, those disappearing would depend on the depth versus euclidean distance test.
